analysis.one_liner: Extends children's online privacy rules to teens, bans targeted ads to kids, and sets security standards for kids' connected devices.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in May 2018 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The Do Not Track Kids Act would have updated the 1998 children's online privacy law in two big ways: it would have covered 13-to-15-year-olds (current law stops at 12) and it would have banned companies from using kids' and teens' personal data to target advertising at them without consent. It would also have required easy-to-read privacy labels on packages of internet-connected devices made for kids, let users delete personal content, and let the Federal Trade Commission block sales of kids' devices that fail basic cybersecurity standards.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers who use websites, apps, and internet-connected toys and gadgets, plus their parents. Parents would get clearer notice and consent rights, teens would get the right to see and delete data collected about them, and families buying connected devices would get a standardized privacy label on the box.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act to 'minors' (ages 13-15), who today have no federal online privacy protection; teens would gain rights to notice, consent, and access to their own data [S3].
Makes it unlawful to use or compile personal information of children or minors for targeted marketing, or to disclose it to third parties for that purpose, without consent [S3].
Requires a standardized privacy dashboard on the packaging of internet-connected devices for kids, telling parents what data is collected, transmitted, retained, and protected [S3].
Directs the FTC to write cybersecurity and data security standards and bars selling connected devices for kids that fail them, with each noncompliant device counted as a separate violation [S3].

Requires operators to build tools letting users erase publicly posted content containing personal information, and lets state attorneys general sue violators and recover restitution for residents [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Websites, apps, and connected-device makers that profit from collecting and monetizing children's and teens' data — chiefly the online advertising ecosystem and manufacturers of internet-connected toys and gadgets — would bear compliance costs and lose access to behaviorally targeted ad revenue from young users.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ad-targeting tech and kids' device makers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would fall hardest on small app and device makers, which must redesign data practices, build deletion tools, and meet FTC device-security standards within roughly a year of enactment [S3].

Services 'directed to minors' must treat every user as a minor, giving the FTC broad rulemaking power to define which sites and apps are covered — a mandate that could lead some companies to restrict or exclude young users rather than comply [S3].

The bill relies on FTC rulemaking for most of its details, so the real-world protections would depend on how the agency at the time defined key terms like 'directed to a minor' and 'targeted marketing' [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For families, the benefits are substantial and the costs are indirect: stronger privacy defaults, an end to profiling kids for ads, and security floors on devices children actually use. The compliance burden on industry is real but is precisely the point — the industries that would pay are the ones that currently profit from collecting young users' data. The main design risk is regulatory breadth, not the direction of the bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and the committee never acted on it before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Markey introduced the bill with Sen. Blumenthal as cosponsor on May 23, 2018 [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online advertising and data-driven tech companies, and makers of internet-connected children's products, avoided new collection limits, an ad-targeting ban, and device security standards. Children and teens gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Do Not Track Kids Act of 2018 on May 23, 2018.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no other senator signed on.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Sen. John Thune, R-SD)
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup, and never voted the bill out, after it was referred on May 23, 2018.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Senate majority (51 Republicans in the 115th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Brought no kids' privacy bill to the floor; the bill never reached a vote in the chamber.

sides.party_line_note: Only the two Democratic senators supported it on the record; with no hearing, vote, or roll call, the partisan shape of broader opposition never showed up in the record.

industries.note: The bill bans using or selling children's and teens' personal information for targeted marketing without consent, cutting off a core revenue stream built on profiling young users. Ordinary users' privacy is the direct cost to this industry.

Makers of internet-connected products for kids would face mandatory privacy labels on packaging, FTC security standards, and a sales ban for devices that fail them. Parents buying the products would get transparency they do not have today.

industries.industry: Websites, apps, and social media platforms
industries.note: Sites and apps directed at minors would owe notice, consent, data-deletion tools, and erasure rights, and could not condition service on surrendering excess data. Services serving young people would carry the compliance burden.

The bill lets operators comply through self-regulatory guidelines written by industry representatives and approved by the FTC, keeping industry-run safe-harbor programs in place — but subject to FTC approval and public reporting.
